facts.claim: In 1923 Eliava founded an institute in Tbilisi devoted to phages.
facts.problem: DOUBTFUL (medium confidence), not blocking. The 1923 founding is the Tbilisi Bacteriological Institute, a general bacteriology institute; the dedicated phage institute (Institute of Bacteriophage) grew out of Eliava's work with d'Herelle in the mid-1930s (c. 1936) and later merged under the Eliava name. The Eliava Institute itself dates its founding to 1923, so this is a common simplification, but 'devoted to phages' from 1923 overstates it.

facts.claim: The phage-resistant form appeared newly sensitive to an antibiotic that had earlier failed.
facts.problem: DOUBTFUL (low to medium confidence), not blocking. In the 2017 case report the post-phage isolates showed increased sensitivity to minocycline, which was already part of his antibiotic regimen alongside the phages rather than a drug that had simply failed earlier. The widely repeated summary (resistance to the phages restored antibiotic sensitivity) matches the passage; 'had earlier failed' is a slight dramatization.

facts.claim: Within as little as half an hour, new viruses fill the cell.
facts.problem: MINOR (medium confidence). 'As little as half an hour' is a reasonable figure for classic T4 (about 25 to 30 minutes), but some well-studied phages such as T7 complete the cycle in roughly 15 to 20 minutes, so the stated minimum is slightly conservative. Not misleading for a student.

facts.claim: In 1934, a long review in the journal of the American Medical Association found most claims unsupported.
facts.problem: STYLE ONLY (high confidence it is otherwise accurate). The Eaton and Bayne-Jones review, JAMA 1934, is real and the characterization is fair. 'journal' should be capitalized as the proper name 'Journal of the American Medical Association' if the author means the title.

MINOR (high confidence). d'Herelle's first phage treatment of patients was in 1919 in Paris, so the 1920s is slightly late as a starting point, though he did treat patients throughout the 1920s. Not wrong as written.
